title: The trumpet
hook: the trumpet is blown, and all rise (39:68)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the questions of the grave, and your line, answer now: an answer held in life holds in the grave.

Some sounds end things. A final whistle. A school bell at three. An alarm at six that ends the night whether you're ready or not. The Qur'an speaks of one sound that ends everything, and then starts it again. In Surah az-Zumar, Pickthall's translation reads: "And the trumpet is blown, and all who are in the heavens and all who are in the earth swoon away, save him whom Allah willeth. Then it is blown a second time, and behold them standing waiting!" Two blasts. One to end, one to raise.
screen: `SOUNDS THAT END THINGS.` → `ONE BLAST TO END.` → `ONE BLAST TO RAISE.`

segments.voice: You heard the trumpet in An-Naba' on day 221; today, both blasts. The Arabic is as-sur, a horn. It sounds in more than one surah, in az-Zumar and again in Ya Sin, in a short, sudden line: and the trumpet is blown. Tradition names the angel who blows it Israfil, though the Qur'an itself doesn't give the name. The first blast brings a swoon over everyone in the heavens and the earth, except whoever Allah wills. Who those exceptions are, the verse leaves open, and commentators have answered in different ways. Then the second blast, and people stand, waiting. How long between the two? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, says: between the two blasts is forty. Someone asks him: forty days? He declines to say. Forty months? He declines. Forty years? He declines again. A companion of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who would not go past what he had said, and readers take that restraint as part of the teaching. Then Ya Sin gives the moment of waking. When the trumpet is blown, people hurry from their graves to their Lord, and their first words, Pickthall again, are: "Woe upon us! Who hath raised us from our place of sleep?" The grave, from the far side, felt like sleep. The answer comes straight back: this is what the Beneficent promised, and the messengers told the truth. So in Muslim teaching the trumpet is not only an ending. It's the sound that means nobody was lost.
screen: `AS-SUR: A HORN, BLOWN TWICE.` · `THE SWOON, SAVE WHOM ALLAH WILLS.` · `FORTY WHAT? HE DECLINED TO SAY.` · then, large: `WHO HATH RAISED US FROM OUR SLEEP?`

segments.voice: Sit low, or lie down, and let your body go heavy, as if you'd been asleep a long time, with the line from Ya Sin in mind: who hath raised us from our place of sleep? Near the end, rise slowly, feet taking your weight, spine lifting, head coming up last; if standing is hard, simply lift your head. Stand still for a few breaths, with the verse from az-Zumar if you pray, or just noticing what it feels like to get up.
The trumpet. As-sur, the horn blown twice, the Qur'an says: once to end, once to raise. Today's word.
Your line: all will rise. Nobody lost, and everyone standing, waiting. Day twelve fifty-six, done.

howItsDone: Muslims believe the trumpet will be blown at the end of the world and again at the resurrection; the verses that describe it are recited in prayer and in sermons about the Last Day.

fork.setup: you're Abu Hurayrah. you've said: between the two blasts is forty. someone asks: forty days? what do you say?
fork.reveal: he declined three times: days, months, years. he would not go past what he had said.

original.note: Arabic: the horn, or trumpet, of the Last Day.

trapdoor: what you thought: the trumpet is a symbol of doom.
what it means: in the Qur'an it is blown twice: once all swoon, then all stand, waiting.
what a scholar hears: as-sur, the open question of who is excepted, and Abu Hurayrah declining to say forty what.

chat.says: Why does the Qur'an mention two trumpet blasts instead of one?
options: One brings a swoon over everyone; the second raises them, standing, waiting.
One is for the believers, and the other blast is for everyone else.
The first marks the night of revelation; the second ends the world.
chat.meaning: In az-Zumar, the first blast brings a swoon over all, save whom Allah wills; then it is blown again, and behold them standing, waiting.

as-sur.meaning: the horn blown on the Day

Abu Hurayrah.meaning: a companion of the Prophet who narrated this hadith
